clinicalScope: Active pulmonary tuberculosis in adults presenting to low‑resource East African hospitals
title: Pulmonary Tuberculosis
subject: Medicine
summary: Tuberculosis is a contagious lung infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It spreads through tiny droplets when an infected person coughs, and it is a leading cause of death worldwide, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) is a chronic granulomatous disease of the lung caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, transmitted by airborne droplets.
b: WHO estimates ~10 million new cases annually; > 80 % occur in low‑ and middle‑income countries.
In East Africa, TB incidence is 200–300 per 100 000 population.
HIV co‑infection triples the risk of progression from latent to active disease.
Most cases are pulmonary; extrapulmonary disease accounts for ~15 %.

sections.h: Causes and risk factors, most likely first
sections.p: Active disease follows inhalation of bacilli and failure of host immunity.
b: Close contact with an untreated smear‑positive case.
HIV infection (CD4 < 200 cells/µL).
Diabetes mellitus, malnutrition, alcoholism, smoking.
Silica exposure (miners, quarry workers) – silico‑tuberculosis.
Use of immunosuppressive drugs (e.g., steroids, anti‑TNF).

sections.p: After inhalation, bacilli are phagocytosed by alveolar macrophages but survive within phagosomes due to a waxy cell wall.
b: Delayed‑type hypersensitivity (type IV) leads to granuloma formation.
Caseating necrosis creates cavitation, especially in upper lobes where oxygen tension is high.
Latent infection persists in granulomas; reactivation occurs when immunity wanes.
HIV impairs CD4‑mediated macrophage activation, accelerating progression.

sections.p: Symptoms develop insidiously over weeks to months.
b: Persistent cough ≥2 weeks, often productive of scant sputum.
Low‑grade fever, night sweats, weight loss (cachexia).
Hemoptysis (usually small) from cavity erosion.
Chest pain pleuritic if pleural involvement.
In HIV‑positive patients, presentation may be atypical or extrapulmonary.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and physical guide the need for microbiology and imaging.
b: Ask about cough duration, sputum characteristics, fever pattern, weight change, night sweats, and exposure to known TB cases.
Screen for HIV, diabetes, smoking, occupational silica.
Inspect for cachexia, clubbing, and chest wall deformities.
Auscultation: crackles over upper zones, possible pleural rub.
Percussion: dullness over cavitary area; shifting dullness suggests pleural effusion.

sections.p: Consider other diseases that cause chronic cough and weight loss.
b: Non‑tuberculous mycobacterial infection (e.g., M. avium complex).
Chronic bacterial pneumonia (e.g., Klebsiella).
Lung cancer, especially squamous cell carcinoma.
Silicosis with secondary infection.
Fungal infections (e.g., histoplasmosis).

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Use a stepwise algorithm that works even when some tests are unavailable.

t.b: Detects acid‑fast bacilli; ≥1 + in 2 of 3 samples confirms active TB.
Detects DNA of M. tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance; positive result = TB, resistance guides regimen.
Shows upper‑lobe infiltrates, cavitation, or miliary pattern; helps assess severity.
Identifies co‑infection; positive result mandates ART integration.
Anemia common; leukocytosis may suggest superinfection.

t.a: If GeneXpert unavailable: sputum culture on Lowenstein‑Jensen medium
t.b: Gold standard but takes 4–8 weeks; positive culture confirms TB.

sections.p: WHO classifies pulmonary TB as ‘new’, ‘relapse’, ‘treatment after failure’, or ‘treatment after loss to follow‑up’. Clinical severity is gauged by symptom burden and radiographic extent.
b: Mild: limited infiltrates, no cavitation, weight loss <10 %.
Moderate: cavitation, weight loss 10–20 %, hemoptysis.
Severe: extensive bilateral disease, massive hemoptysis, respiratory failure.
Miliary or disseminated disease counts as severe regardless of chest findings.

sections.p: Co‑morbidities and local resource limits affect diagnosis and outcome.
b: HIV may produce atypical radiographs (e.g., lower‑lobe infiltrates).
Diabetes predisposes to treatment failure and relapse.
Concurrent bacterial pneumonia can mask TB signs.
Limited laboratory capacity may force reliance on clinical scoring.

sections.p: Standardised short‑course therapy (6 months) is recommended; modify only for drug resistance or intolerance.
b: Intensive phase (2 months): isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol (HRZE).
Continuation phase (4 months): isoniazid + rifampicin (HR).
Directly observed therapy (DOT) ensures adherence in low‑resource settings.
Monitor liver function, visual acuity (ethambutol), and sputum conversion at 2 months.
If rifampicin resistance detected, switch to second‑line regimen per national guidelines.

sections.p: Early recognition of complications reduces mortality.
b: Hemoptysis >100 mL/24 h → urgent bronchoscopy or embolisation.
Pleural effusion with respiratory compromise → thoracentesis.
Miliary TB → start therapy immediately; consider adjunctive steroids if CNS involvement.
Drug‑induced hepatotoxicity (ALT/AST >3× ULN with symptoms) → pause hepatotoxic drugs.
Treatment failure (positive sputum at 5 months) → assess adherence, resistance.
Pregnant women: avoid streptomycin; HRZE is safe.
Children <5 years: higher risk of disseminated disease; use weight‑based dosing.
Elderly: monitor for drug toxicity, comorbidities.
HIV‑positive: start ART 2 weeks after TB therapy, unless CD4 < 50 cells/µL (then start within 2 weeks).

sections.p: With proper treatment, cure rates exceed 85 % even in low‑resource settings.
b: Sputum smear conversion by 2 months predicts good outcome.
Schedule follow‑up visits at 2, 5, and 6 months to assess adherence and side effects.
BCG vaccination at birth provides partial protection against severe pediatric TB.
Infection control: cough etiquette, ventilation, and isolation of smear‑positive patients.
Contact tracing and prophylactic isoniazid for children <5 years.

sections.p: Be aware of false‑negative or non‑specific findings.
b: Smear microscopy may be negative in early disease or HIV; rely on GeneXpert or culture.
Chest X‑ray can be normal in HIV patients despite active TB.
Elevated ESR is non‑specific; use in conjunction with clinical picture.
Rifampicin resistance on GeneXpert requires confirmatory line‑probe assay before changing regimen.

whenToSeekHelp: Persistent fever despite 2 months of therapy

faq.q: Why is GeneXpert preferred over smear microscopy?
faq.a: It detects TB DNA rapidly and identifies rifampicin resistance, improving early appropriate therapy.

faq.q: Can TB be cured without DOT?
faq.a: Cure rates drop markedly without supervised therapy because of poor adherence and resistance development.

faq.q: Is a normal chest X‑ray enough to rule out TB?
faq.a: No; especially in HIV patients, TB can be radiographically occult, so microbiology is essential.

exam: What is the next best step after a patient with a 3‑week cough and weight loss has a negative sputum smear but high clinical suspicion? — Obtain GeneXpert or send sputum for culture; consider chest X‑ray.
How does HIV infection alter the radiographic appearance of pulmonary TB? — It often produces lower‑lobe infiltrates, less cavitation, and may be normal.

Explain why rifampicin resistance on GeneXpert mandates a change in regimen. — Rifampicin is a cornerstone of the 6‑month regimen; resistance predicts multidrug‑resistant TB requiring second‑line drugs.
A patient on HRZE develops jaundice and ALT 250 U/L. What should you do? — Stop all hepatotoxic drugs, assess for other causes, and restart with a modified regimen once liver enzymes improve.
Which clinical feature most strongly predicts cavitary disease? — Persistent cough with hemoptysis and weight loss >10 %.

Describe the infection‑control measures needed in a crowded ward with a smear‑positive TB patient. — Place patient in a well‑ventilated area or isolation, use surgical masks for staff and visitors, encourage cough etiquette.
Why is DOT especially important in low‑resource settings? — It overcomes barriers to adherence such as cost, travel, and health‑system gaps, reducing resistance.
What is the rationale for giving ethambutol in the intensive phase? — It prevents emergence of resistance while awaiting susceptibility results.

How would you differentiate pulmonary TB from non‑tuberculous mycobacterial infection on sputum testing? — GeneXpert is specific for M. tuberculosis; culture with species identification differentiates NTM.

A 30‑year‑old HIV‑positive man on ART presents with fever, cough, and a chest X‑ray showing diffuse micronodules. What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management? — Miliary TB; start full anti‑TB regimen promptly and consider adjunctive steroids if CNS involvement is suspected.
